Having done this, I detached a few additional loops from the rim, slipped in another section of cloth, and joined the loosened loops to their corresponding buttons. By proceeding thus, I could introduce the entire upper portion of the bag between the netting and the hoop. Clearly, the hoop must now fall inside the car, while the car's full weight, together with everything it contained, would be sustained solely by the buttons. At first glance this might appear a precarious support; it was, however, nothing of the sort, for the buttons were exceedingly stout in themselves and stood so near together that each bore only a trifling share of the total burden. Indeed, even had the car and its contents weighed three times as much, I should have felt no apprehension. I next lifted the hoop once more inside the gum-elastic covering, supporting it at almost its original elevation with three light poles made ready for this purpose. Naturally, this served to hold the upper part of the bag open and maintain the lower portion of the netting in its proper position. Nothing remained except to secure the mouth of the enclosure, which I easily effected by collecting the folds of the fabric and twisting them tightly together on the inner side with a sort of fixed tourniquet.

“Three round panes of thick yet transparent glass had been set into the sides of the covering now arranged about the car. Through these I could readily survey my surroundings in every horizontal direction. The section of fabric that constituted the bottom contained a fourth window of the same description, aligned with a small opening in the floor of the car itself. Through it I could look directly downwards. But the particular method of fastening the opening above, and the folds it necessarily produced in the fabric, had made it impossible to fit any corresponding arrangement overhead; I could therefore expect no view of objects immediately above me. This was, of course, of slight importance: even if I had contrived to insert a window at the top, the balloon itself would have rendered it useless.

“Some twelve inches beneath one of the side windows there was a round aperture, eight inches across, furnished with a brass rim whose inner edge was cut to receive the turns of a screw. Into this rim I screwed the condenser's large tube, the body of the apparatus remaining, as a matter of course, inside the gum-elastic chamber.

For years Dorian Gray remained under the book's influence. Perhaps it would be truer to say that he never tried to escape it. He ordered no fewer than nine copies of the first edition from Paris, printed on large paper, and had each bound in a different colour. They would match his different moods and the shifting desires of a nature he sometimes seemed almost unable to control. The hero, a remarkable young Parisian who combined romantic feeling with a scientific cast of mind, seemed to show Dorian an early image of himself. In fact, he felt that the whole book told the story of his life before he had lived it.

In one respect he was luckier than the novel's extraordinary hero. He never experienced, or had any reason to experience, the young Parisian's strange fear of mirrors, shiny metal, and still water. That fear had begun early, when the young man's apparently remarkable good looks suddenly faded. Dorian read the later part of the book with an almost cruel delight. Perhaps cruelty belongs to almost every kind of joy, as it certainly belongs to every pleasure. Those later pages told the truly tragic, though somewhat exaggerated, story of the hero's grief and despair. He had lost in himself the very thing he had valued most in other people and in the world.

Dorian's own astonishing beauty, which had captivated Basil Hallward and so many others, never seemed to fade. Even people who had heard the worst accusations against him could not believe anything disgraceful about him once they saw his face. From time to time strange rumours about the way he lived spread through London and became the talk of the clubs. Yet he always looked like someone the world had left untouched. Men telling crude stories fell silent when Dorian Gray walked into a room. His innocent face seemed to reproach them. Simply being near him reminded them of the innocence they themselves had spoiled. They wondered how anyone so charming and graceful could have remained unstained by an age so full of corruption and desire.

He often came home after one of the long, mysterious absences that led his friends, and those who thought they were his friends, to make such strange guesses about him. Then he would creep upstairs to the locked room and unlock the door with the key he now always carried. Holding a mirror, he would stand before the portrait Basil Hallward had painted of him. His eyes moved between the wicked, ageing face on the canvas and the beautiful young face laughing back at him from the bright glass.

“Then you believe your master really received a bite from the beetle, and that this bite caused his illness?”

“I don't believe noffin—I knows it. Why he dream so much 'bout goole, unless de goole-bug done bit him? I's heard tell of dem goole-bugs afore now.”

“But what tells you that gold is what he dreams of?”

“What tells me? Why, he talks of it when he sleeps—dat's what tells me.”

“Well, Jup, you may be right; but what happy circumstance has brought me the honour of your company to-day?”

“What you mean, massa?”

“Have you brought a message from Mr. Legrand?”

“No, massa, I brought dis here letter;” and Jupiter gave me a note to the following effect:

“MY DEAR —— Why has it been so long since you visited me? I trust you have not been foolish enough to resent some slight abruptness on my part; but no, that is hardly likely. Since our last meeting I have had much reason for anxiety. There is something I wish to tell you, although I hardly know how to express it, or even whether I ought to speak of it.

“For several days I have been rather unwell, and poor old Jup, with his kindly intended attentions, vexes me almost past bearing. Can you credit it? The other day he actually provided himself with an enormous stick to punish me for eluding him and passing the day alone among the mainland hills. I firmly believe that only my sickly appearance spared me a beating.

“I have added nothing to my cabinet since we last met.

“If you can possibly arrange it, come across with Jupiter. Pray come. I want to see you this very night on an important matter. Believe me, it is a matter of the utmost importance.

“Always yours, WILLIAM LEGRAND.”

Something in the note's tone made me profoundly uneasy. Its entire manner was markedly unlike Legrand's usual style. What could occupy his dreams? What fresh whim had seized his restless mind? What conceivable affair could require him to conduct ‘business of the utmost importance’? Jupiter's report offered little reassurance. I feared that the unrelenting strain of adversity had finally disturbed my friend's reason. I therefore made ready, without an instant's hesitation, to go with the black man.

When we arrived at the wharf, I observed a scythe and three spades, seemingly all new, at the bottom of the boat in which we were about to embark.

“What does all this signify, Jup?”
